input: Learn to read a topographic hiking map

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Topo map reading spans many sub-skills (contour lines, elevation, symbols, scale, grid references, route planning). Knowing which specific skills to focus on prevents an overwhelming or under-scoped plan.
Whether this is for the user alone or for a group (e.g., family, scouts, hiking club) changes the depth, format, and social dimension of the learning.
The type of terrain and upcoming hike (mountain, forest, desert) determines which map features matter most and gives a concrete practice target.
The available time before the user needs this skill (a weekend trip next week vs. a long-term goal) dramatically changes the pace and depth of the plan.
People learn navigation skills very differently — hands-on field practice, video tutorials, books, or structured courses. Matching the plan to their learning style maximises retention.
The user's definition of 'done' could range from casually understanding contour lines to confidently navigating off-trail without a phone. This sets the target level of proficiency.
Whether they already have a physical map, a compass, or access to digital tools (e.g., CalTopo, AllTrails) determines the immediate first step and what resources need to be sourced.

gold.taskTitle: Learn to read a topographic hiking map
gold.taskDescription: The user wants to develop the skill of reading and interpreting topographic maps for hiking purposes.

questions.title: Which specific topo skills do you most need to master?
questions.description: Identify whether the focus is on reading contour lines, understanding scale and elevation gain, decoding map symbols, plotting grid references, or planning a full route — or all of the above.

questions.title: Are you learning this for yourself or with others?
questions.description: Clarify whether the plan is for solo self-study or includes teaching/learning alongside a partner, family member, or group.

questions.title: Do you have a specific hike or terrain type in mind?
questions.description: Knowing the target terrain (alpine, forest, desert canyon, etc.) or a concrete upcoming trip gives a real map to practice on and makes the skills immediately relevant.

questions.title: How soon do you need to be confident with this skill?
questions.description: Establish the deadline or urgency — a trip in two weeks requires a very different plan than a gradual skill-build over several months.

questions.title: How do you learn best — hands-on, videos, or reading?
questions.description: Determine the preferred learning style so the plan can prioritise field exercises, online tutorials, illustrated guides, or a formal navigation course accordingly.

questions.title: What does confidently reading a map look like for you?
questions.description: Define the end goal — for example, being able to follow a marked trail using a map, navigate to a summit cross-country, or lead others on a route without relying on a phone.

questions.title: Do you already have a map, compass, or navigation apps?
questions.description: Find out what physical and digital tools the user currently owns so the plan can start from their existing setup rather than assuming resources they may need to acquire first.
